identification: Anonymous prose tract "De regiminibus tractantes", after about 1245; a source or sibling of Gutolf of Heiligenkreuz, Summa grammatica ch. XVI; not identified

Readings are a research subagent's; coordinator did not recheck.

catalogue_title: Alexander of Hales, Summa Theologica; unidentified theological text
identification: Wrapper made from four manuscripts: Summa Halensis III (as catalogued), Juvencus with glosses, a Lenten gradual, and an unidentified text on giving out of pietas
note: Front strip: six consecutive lines match Summa Halensis III, exposition of the Nicene Creed, Quaracchi IV p. 1133 (snippets). Sideways sheets: Juvencus, Evangeliorum libri, Praefatio 4-10 and I 10-14, with glosses (Corpus Corporum; from the first reading, not re-read). Neumed pieces: gradual, Lent IV and Passion Sunday (from the first reading). Back strip unidentified after three passes: a preaching text on pietas shown in giving, with numbered divisions, Luke 11:42 and Valerius Maximus V.1.9 and V.1.8 in the form Cessolis gives them ("capiti reponi iussit"), which suggests a date after about 1300. Not the Summa Halensis (its index cites Valerius once, elsewhere), not Cessolis, John of Wales, Peraldus, Servasanctus's Antidotarius or the sermons printed under Bonaventure's name (searched inside; few page images). Untested: Stephen of Bourbon, distinction collections, Servasanctus's unprinted works.

institution: Chicago, University of Chicago Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center
identification: Short Sunday gospel sermons, Dom. III-V and IX-XI after Pentecost: a reworded short redaction of the anonymous South German cycle called "Ungarus" or "Cordulus"; no witness with this wording found
note: Each sermon on the bifolium follows the corresponding sermon of the cycle point by point, with the same authorities and distinctive matter (the temple with eight steps that are the beatitudes; Christ weeping three times; the five effects of the word), as read on page images of Leipzig UB Ms 720 ff. 83v-90r, Freiburg UB Hs. 138 and München UB 4° Cod. ms. 882 ff. 49r-58v by a research reader; the coordinator compared the Duo homines opening with Leipzig f. 90r. None of the three matches for five consecutive lines: the fragment is compressed and reworded, drops the opening "tria" division, and agrees now with one witness, now with another. The witnesses are reported to have no uniform text. Not opened: Frankfurt UB Ms. Carm. 26 (digitised, behind a bot check; the likeliest short form), Clm 3088, Stuttgart HB I 90, Berlin lat. qu. 699, Clm 16036, 8210, 21542 (not digitised). The fragment's incipits are in none of the nine Schneyer volumes. Not a commentary on Luke.

identification: Servasanctus de Faventia, Antidotarius animae: the castle of the soul, chapters on feast days, on restraining touch and on the sixth gate
note: The two leaves are consecutive and follow the Louvain print (Johannes de Westfalia, GW M41855), fols. xlv verso to xlvii verso, in order: three stretches and several rubrics compared with page images of the Wolfenbüttel copy by a research reader, the sixth-gate opening by the coordinator. Includes the author's Faenza miracle. Found only after the second leaf was read and Google Books search matched "porta interioris affectus"; the first pass, on one leaf, took it for a Decalogue treatise. Small variants. The exempla come from Martinus Polonus and Gregory.

institution: Chicago, University of Chicago Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center
identification: Rhymed verse rendering, with rubrics and canon-law gloss, of Raymond of Penyafort, Summa de casibus I.1 De simonia; the versification is not identified
note: Six units on both sides follow Raymond's paragraphs VIII-X in order (Verona 1744 pp. 12-14, OCR), and the marginal gloss gives Raymond's allegations. Not Adam's Summula (three prints searched; BnF lat. 15162 f. 56r read on the page is Adam's). No verse found in Google Books, archive.org or Corpus Corporum. The Villers chronicle says Arnulf of Louvain versified the Summa and that work is reported unrecovered; nothing survives to compare, so this is not an attribution.

identification: John of Abbeville, sermons for saints' days: Sicut exaltavit Moyses serpentem and Ego quasi vitis (Nativity of the Virgin)
note: All four columns are one continuous passage agreeing with Charleville-Mézières BM 218, ff. 38r-40r (IRHT microfilm page images), about 120 lines in three stretches read by a research reader; the coordinator compared two places on the images. Schneyer 3 p. 529 nos. 271-272 (snippets). Work unprinted. The side labelled v precedes the side labelled r. A sermon collection, not a biblical commentary.

identification: Abbreviated scholastic notes, including the question whether the intellect can know truth without special divine illumination; not identified
note: Photographed upside down; the first reader gave only a layout survey and a second isolated reader read a rotated packet. One passage answers the question as Duns Scotus does (Ord. I d.3), so notes on I Sent. d.3 in a Scotist order are a lead. The other side is abraded. No verbatim match.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Question-commentary on Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), close to the Cologne Copulata; the commentary is not identified
note: The "amator sapientie ... desiderator" argument and reply, and the "nullum animal currit" argument, run parallel in content and order to Lambertus de Monte's Copulata (Cologne 1487 and 1494, OCR) in other words; one argument on totum integrale is Versor's. No printed commentary matches verbatim for five lines: also tested Johannes de Magistris, Tartaret, Marsilius and an anonymous Scotist exposition (OCR); Bricot's OCR was too corrupt to test; Gerardus de Harderwijk and the Louvain commentaries were not found online. The subject of the first argument is read "rusticus" or "iustus"; the letters are ambiguous. Probably a student reportatio of Cologne Thomist teaching.

identification: Scholastic sermon on James 1:25 "non auditor obliviosus factus sed factor operis"; not identified
note: About half the surface is illegible at the available resolution. Readable members ("premium copiosum ... premium beatificum"; "quelibet res habet propriam operacionem") matched nothing in Google Books, archive.org or Corpus Corporum. Schneyer by theme not tested.

identification: Pseudo-Haymo, Liverani homiliary (anonymous Carolingian reworking of Haymo of Auxerre): homilies on Mark 8:1-9 (Barré 55, Liverani XLII), Matthew 7:15-21 (Barré 56, Liverani XLIV, end) and Luke 16:1-9 (Barré 57, Liverani XLV, start)
note: Four passages on fols. 4r, 4v, 5r and 5v agree in sequence and distinctive wording with the collection printed by Liverani in 1863 and with Paris, BnF, Latin 3806, fols. 137r-138r; a research reader compared two with Liverani through Google Books snippets and two with page images of Latin 3806. The leaf differs in detail from both witnesses (reworded incipit of the steward homily, some sentences absent, readings shared now with one, now with the other), so the recension is undetermined. The bifolium belongs to the same manuscript as NAL 2317 ff. 6 and 7 (F-1szi, F-vpe8). The catalogue had already noted that fol. 4r is close to Haymo, PL 118, 637-639. The coordinator read the fol. 4v column b passage on the image; Liverani was not seen as page images; no human review.

identification: Pseudo-Haymo, Liverani homiliary (anonymous Carolingian reworking of Haymo of Auxerre): homily on Matthew 6:24-33 (Barré 67, Liverani LIII), ravens and lilies
note: The ravens passage on fol. 6r and the Solomon and lilies passage on fol. 6v ('lilium in uirginibus rosam in martiribus uiolam in confessoribus') agree in sequence and wording with Paris, BnF, Latin 3806, fols. 163v-165r, read as page images by a research reader, and with Liverani's 1863 print read through Google Books snippets; the coordinator read the lilies passage on the image. The leaf is a homily, not the biblical commentary of the catalogue title. Its lilies section is shorter and partly reworded against both witnesses, and two of its glosses were not found in either, so the recension is undetermined. It belongs to the same manuscript as NAL 2317 ff. 4-5 and 7 (F-kr2n, F-vpe8). Liverani was not seen as page images; no human review.

identification: Pseudo-Haymo, Liverani homiliary (anonymous Carolingian reworking of Haymo of Auxerre): homilies on Luke 7:11-16 (Barré 68, Liverani LIV, end) and Luke 14:1-11 (Barré 69, Liverani LV, start)
note: Three passages of the Nain homily (mother as the Church, bearers of the bier as flatterers, 'Dedit illum matri sue') and the opening of the Luke 14 homily ('peritissimus piscator ... auceps uel uenator') agree in sequence and wording with Paris, BnF, Latin 3806, fols. 170r-171r and 175r-175v, read as page images by a research reader, and with Liverani's 1863 print read through Google Books snippets; the coordinator read 'Mater autem huius defuncti ... filios gignere non cessat' on the image. The leaf is from a homiliary, not the biblical commentary of the catalogue title, and belongs to the same manuscript as NAL 2317 ff. 4-5 and 6 (F-kr2n, F-1szi). The Luke 14 homily lacks the proem both witnesses have and opens 'Quociescumque legimus', nearer Haymo's own text, so the recension is undetermined. Liverani was not seen as page images; no human review.

identification: Pseudo-Galen, Liber de dynamidiis (Juntine 'Liber alter de dynamidiis'): De catharticis to De opio (f. 104) and recipes Contra vitia faciei to Electuarium dianthu (f. 105)
note: Four passages on three faces (agaric and cnicus, opium and omphacomel, impetigo and morphea recipes, Diamoron for the throat) agree in wording and order with the 1625 Giunta print, read as page images by a research reader; the coordinator read f. 105r lines 10-20 on the image against the print text. The leaf has an older form than the corrected print: it keeps 'Diamoron batinum' and 'mororum bati', lacks the print's glosses, and on f. 105r has one recipe the print lacks and lacks two it has. Two passages were also compared with images of Cologny, Cod. Bodmer 58 (14th c.), which shares the leaf's wording against the print. Oribasius Latinus, Synopsis I 17, was tested and rejected. Most lines rest on the image-only first reading, the recension is undetermined, and there has been no human review.

identification: Not identified
note: The catalogued fragment is fol. A, a small leaf from a different manuscript bound with the Priscian endleaves (record F-fwl6), plus a stub. About 25 lines of pale brown writing run at right angles under a mirror-image offset of the Priscian, and only isolated words could be read (embolism..., putatur, libra?), none secure in sequence, so nothing could be searched. Contrast stretching and single colour channels did not help; ultraviolet or multispectral imaging probably would. The first image-only reading and the first research pass read the facing Priscian page by the coordinator's mistake; that page is Institutiones XIV 30-32, as the catalogue already says of F-fwl6.

identification: Abbreviated sermon book drawing on Berthold of Regensburg (Rusticanus de Dominicis, 14th Sunday after Pentecost; Rusticanus de Sanctis 3) and Conrad of Saxony; the compilation is not identified
note: Leaves 88r-86v carry Berthold's sermon on threefold fidelity and the opening of his sermon on the three crosses, both abridged and reworded; a research reader matched the first on page images of Freiburg UB Hs. 152 f. 111v (full text) and Munich Clm 8739 ff. 205v-206r (another abridgement), and the second on a page image of Leipzig UB Ms 498 f. 5v plus snippets of Hoetzl's 1882 edition. The fragment replaces Berthold's ending of the first sermon with an unsourced instruction on the Passion by the canonical hours, and drops St Francis from the second. Leaves 87r-89v carry an All Souls sermon built on the ps.-Bonaventure / Conrad of Saxony De mortuis III (1596 print, OCR) with large additions; its containing work is not identified. The abridged collection itself is not located and is not the one in Clm 8739. Recorded as partial because the sermons are reworked and the book they come from is unknown: the Berthold texts are its sources, not yet the identified work. The coordinator compared 88r lines 1-7 with the Freiburg page image. No human review; catalogue date and origin not reassessed.

identification: Henricus de Piro, Super Institutiones, on Inst. 1.7-1.8 and 1.21-1.24
note: Six passages on five of the 22 faces (fragm. a-b recto and verso, q-r recto, s-t recto last paragraph, u-v recto) agree in wording, order and legal citations with the Cologne c. 1481 edition (GW 12256), read by a research reader from page images of the Munich copy; the coordinator checked fragm. u-v recto lines 1-10 on the image. Differences are minor (sint/fuerint, an added videre, Continuatio/Continuatur, usque ad/in, singular or plural of ultima voluntas), and the manuscript leaves the title headings blank. The other 17 faces were only surveyed, the lettering of the leaves does not follow the text order, and only one of three incunable editions was compared. Whether the leaves were copied from a print or are an independent manuscript witness is not determined. No human review.

identification: Johannes Versor, Quaestiones super libros Posteriorum Aristotelis, book II qq. 1, 2, 8 (reworded against the Cologne prints)
note: All four pages of the bifolium follow Versor's questions on Posterior Analytics II in question titles, order of arguments and conclusions and long runs of wording; seven passages were set against page images of the Quentell print of about 1487 (BSB bsb00044403, scans 100, 101, 110), and question 8 was read again in the 1497 print. A research reader reread five of the passages on the image with the source at hand and the coordinator read the magnanimity passage (fol. 2v col. a); two passages rest on the image-only first reading; no human review. The manuscript rewords and shortens the printed text throughout and drifts in places towards Thomas Aquinas's wording, so it is a version or reworking of Versor, not a straight copy. Thomas (source layer) and the Cologne Copulata novae logicae (running exposition without these questions; it also has the Hercules gloss) were read at the same place and excluded as the containing work. Not tested: Welker 1486 Nova logica, non-Cologne editions, Harderwijck, Tartaretus; lower inner columns are lost.

identification: Student notes of a scholastic philosophy course (physics running into natural theology, with some logic), by a Dutch-speaking writer; not identified
note: Not metaphysics in the narrow sense. One hand throughout 37 leaves: questions on whole and parts, the definition of nature, nature and art (with a passage on alchemy naming Raymond Lull), the four causes, creation as a 'modus substantialis', God's concurrence with secondary causes and a section 'De Praedeterminatione' arguing against physical predetermination; then, after blank pages, logic notes and a second run headed 'De Physica' (prime matter, substantial form, 'De unione'), breaking off at a catchword. A three-line entry on fol. 13r mixes Latin and Dutch. No title, date, place, owner or professor's name was read; fol. 21r opens with two names after 'illustrissimus ... vir doctissimus' that could not be made out. The doctrine and vocabulary look later than the catalogue's 1551-1600, which was not assessed further. Helper readers covered the top half of each page only. The record's manifest serves the first three images again in place of canvases 9-13, 24-28 and 34-37; the right images were fetched by correcting the file number. Compton Carleton and Cornaeus were searched without a match; Arriaga, Hurtado, Oviedo, the Conimbricenses and the Louvain and Douai dictated courses are untested.

identification: Exposition of Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), on the topics from opposites; not a musical treatise; the exposition is not identified
note: No musical term occurs on the leaf or its three sibling leaves (F-hwsh, F-21br, F-jfv6, same hand). The leaf works through the topics from relative, contrary, privative and contradictory opposites in the order of Peter of Spain's Tractatus V, chapters 27-31 ('Contraria mediata sunt inter que aliquid est medium ut album et nigrum ... immediata ut sanum et egrum'; 'si una fuerit vera altera erit falsa'), paraphrasing and adding matter Peter lacks (a topic 'a disparatis', the proviso of 'constantia subiecti'). F-21br has the topics from the greater and the lesser, and F-hwsh ends 'Et sic est finis quinti tractatus'. Peter's text was compared only through archive.org search snippets of two lending-restricted editions. No printed commentary was matched; about half the lines rest on the first reading. Probably classroom notes.

institution: Victoria, B.C., University of Victoria Libraries
catalogue_title: Medical recipes and poems | includes poetic list of women's faults
identification: Cibaldone (anonymous Italian verse regimen, "Libro terzo dello Almansore"), end of the chapter on bathing, fol. 38r col. a
note: The Italian verses on the recto are the last three and a half stanzas of the Cibaldone and end the work, followed by the scribe's explicit. A research reader compared nineteen manuscript lines with page images of the last two pages of the first edition, [Vicenza, about 1475], Florence BNC copy: same stanzas in the same order, but the manuscript has its own spelling, lacks one couplet and keeps rhymes the print lacks; whether it descends from a print or from a manuscript of the poem is not determined. Lines 1-15 were reread on the image; lines 16-19 were corrected from the print. The Frederick powder on the recto is a longer version of a recipe printed by Sudhoff in 1915 (OCR only), and the list of women's faults on the verso reuses three known sayings but is unidentified as a whole. No human review.

catalogue_title: Table of contents of a lost or unidentified book
identification: Contents leaf of a composite volume of the canons of St Leonard near Liège, after 1492; entries 2, 3, 6 and 9 matched to works or editions; the volume itself is not securely traced
note: The leaf lists ten pieces of one bound volume. The catalogue already recognises a composite volume with prints and links entries 2 (Beissel, Rosacea corona, Antwerp, Bac) and 6 (Tabulare de Carmelo, Alost, Martens) to incunables. Added here: entry 3 is Wimpfeling and Gaguin, Epistole et carmina, Cologne, Renchen, after 20 February 1492 (title-page image of the Munich copy), which dates the list; entry 9 is the Life of Gerard of Brogne; entry 8 matches a sermon printed under Gerson's name by title only; entries 4, 5, 7 and 10 are unmatched. Candidates for surviving pieces, not established: Den Haag, KB, KW 169 G 7 (Gregory, Dialogi, Louvain, Westfalia, with the priory's ownership note, which is its standard formula and occurs in other books) and Brussels, KBR, ms. II 734 (a Life of Gerard with the leaf's title and nearly its format). Both were bought at the 1884 Vergauwen sale, which also had a Beissel and a Tabulare, but shared ownership, similar size, one sale and matching nineteenth-century bindings do not show that these copies were bound in this volume, and the edition of entry 1 rests on that link. Known only from MEI, the Brussels catalogue (OCR) and the sale catalogue; neither book was seen. Comparing paper, edges, sewing holes and offsets of those two books with the leaf would settle it.

identification: Breviary strip: hymn Martyris Christi colimus triumphum (as catalogued) and a second, unidentified hymn for St Lawrence
note: The first hymn is confirmed against Daniel, Thesaurus hymnologicus IV p. 140 (OCR), as the catalogue already names it. After the rubric "In primo No[cturno]" a second hymn in iambic dimeter follows ("... Laurentius dignus sac... qui vicit ignium ... Hic unus est e... columnis lucidis ... simulque fecit opifex"). One strophe opens like "Quid furis, hostis impie" in Devota mente socii (Analecta Hymnica 14 no. 103) but continues differently; an OCR scan of all 55 volumes of Analecta Hymnica, Cantus Index, Corpus Corporum and Google Books found nothing else. About twenty letters are lost at the left of every line, so the incipit is unknown. Sister fragments in Tübingen UB (Mm IV 1, Mm V 28, Gb 55 a.4), which may have the text entire, are not digitised.

catalogue_title: Unidentified commentary on Ieremias | XXXII, 35-41; XXXVI, 3-16.
identification: Literal commentary on Jeremiah 32:35-41 and 36:2-9 built on Hugh of St Cher's Postilla; the work is not identified
note: The glosses and their order follow Hugh of St Cher (Gloss-e text): 'ut initiarent id est dedicarent', 'idolum Ammonitarum', 'sic construe ... propter ista scilicet mala', and at chapter 36 'Composuit Salomon ... veritate plenos' followed by 'verbum Dei non est alligatum'. It is not Hugh's own literal layer: it adds a division of the text at 32:36 that Hugh lacks and omits his 'Triplici ratione' at 36:4. Thomas Aquinas, Nicholas of Lyra and the Glossa ordinaria were compared and excluded. The later postills built on Hugh (William of Luxi, William of Alton, Nicholas Gorran) are unedited or not online and were not tested; Luxi is the first to check. Script is tiny and many readings are uncertain.

catalogue_title: Neumed Easter dialogue and canonistic miscellany
identification: Florilegium of short extracts (gloss on Wisdom 1:7, Peter Damian against clerical marriage, the five reasons for St Peter's tonsure); the compilation is not identified
note: The prose column strings together three extracts. The tonsure passage has the reworked form with both closing sentences that Munich Clm 4654 f. 62v has (compared on the page image) and that Fournier reports for Collectio XII partium III.277; two sentences headed 'Petrus Damiani ... in uxores clericorum' match his letter against clerical marriage as quoted in MGH Libelli de lite I p. 354; the gloss on Wisdom 1:7 has no source found. No manuscript or work with the three together was found; Corpus Corporum searches of the twelfth-century liturgical handbooks were negative. The neumed Easter dialogue on the other half is in leonine hexameters ('Cur estis tristes, quid queritis hic mulieres') and none of its verses was found in the searchable sources; Lipphardt and Young could not be searched, so it may or may not be edited.

catalogue_title: Latin commentary on an unidentified theological treatise
identification: Late scholastic logic course: questions on Aristotle's Categories and a lemma exposition of Posterior Analytics I; not identified
note: Not theology, as catalogued. The strips have chapter-numbered questions on the whole Categories ('Circa quintum capitulum. Queritur primo utrum qualitas bene diffinitur', 'utrum habitus et dispositio sint prima species qualitatis') closing with a fixed 'Conclusio responsalis ... est a philosopho bene assignata ... Sed oportet dicere ad rationes', and an exposition of Posterior Analytics I with 'Istud est N capitulum huius tractatus in quo philosophus'. The format is the Paris school type: Petrus Tartaretus (snippets) and Johannes de Magistris (Heidelberg 1488, page images) are the nearest and are not the text; Versor, the Cologne Copulata, Harderwijck, Parreut, Friesner, Bricot and Nicholas of Amsterdam were also rejected. About twelve of 76 faces were read closely, the rest surveyed by headings. Usingen, Trutfetter and Hundt untested; it may be an unprinted course.

institution: Leuven, Archief van de Abdij van Park
identification: Preaching text on preparing the heart, akin to Nicolaus de Byard's distinctio "Preparare"; not identified
note: Both faces were read in full: a run of "Item debemus preparare corda nostra sicut ..." comparisons (a host readying his lodging for a great guest, Esther dressing for the king, a vessel washed by confession, Judith). The same scheme and proof-texts (Ps 9:38, Sir 2:20, Jer 4:14, 1 Reg 7:3) stand in compressed form in Nicolaus de Byard's Distinctiones under "Preparare" (Yale, Beinecke MS 746, ff. 170v-171r, page images) and in his Summa de abstinentia, chapter "De preparatione" (1518 print, OCR), but the wording and order differ and several of the fragment's passages are absent, so this is kinship, not the work. Byard's sermon on 1 Reg 7:3 (incipit "Dicitur vulgariter"), the likeliest fuller version, was not reachable: Angers BM 251, listed under his name, proved on its page images to be a different collection, and BnF lat. 12419, Avranches 133 and Laon have no images online. Google Books, Corpus Corporum, archive.org and the Munich full-text search found no sentence of the fragment.

identification: Not identified
note: The catalogued item is the narrow strip stuck upside down along the rear pastedown; about 19 line-ends of five to nine letters are legible (credo, [h]abemus, ministerio, celi et ter[re], inquit), too little to match. The computus leaf beneath it, read by the first reader, is a separate item (apparently record F-xr53): an anonymous Carolingian text on lunar regulars and epacts that also stands in Munich Clm 22307 f. 193r.

identification: Johannes Matthaeus, Concionum dispositiones (Wittenberg, 1581; 2nd ed. 1590), end of the outline "De templorum dedicatione" (handwritten copy of pp. 865-868)
note: Four paper pieces are a pen copy of the last four pages of a printed book, with its running titles, page numbers 865-868 and signatures Kkk and Kkk2. A research reader compared six passages from all four pages with page images of the 1581 Wittenberg edition (part 2, pp. 408-412), where the text agrees closely, including the Epilogus, the Greek doxology and the print's slip "1. Pet. 3"; the coordinator compared the Epilogus and doxology on the fragment image with the 1581 page image of p. 412. Differences: page and line division, and a few words (significabat for significat, purgarit for purgaverit, ita for ibi facere). The page numbers fit the catalogued collation of the 1590 edition (VD16 E 4591: 8 leaves, 868 pages, 2 leaves), which was not seen, so the edition copied is inferred and the variants are unassigned. Aretius, De encaeniis, and Legenda aurea c. 182 are Matthaeus's sources, not the work copied; no human review.

identification: Notes on the dialectical topic of etymology following Melanchthon's Erotemata dialectices IV; not found in print
note: One unfinished page says that the 'autor', after definition and its parts, 'statim subiungit Etymologiam' and then 'coniugata et casus', which is the order of topics in Melanchthon's Erotemata dialectices book IV. This is agreement of structure only: no sentence was found in print through Google Books or the Munich full-text search, and a textbook derived from Melanchthon would give the same order. The parchment cover in the record's later images belongs to record F-x06a, already catalogued as Cicero, De natura deorum II; the manifests of this record and F-v0qx both carry those images.

identification: Abridged or adapted text built on Guido de Monte Rocherii, Manipulus curatorum, pars I, tract. V, cap. 3-4; containing text not established
note: Both columns of the verso follow the Manipulus in order, collated by a research reader against page images of the Cologne 1476 print. The leaf departs in substance: the preamble of cap. 4 is cut to about three lines, the author's "reputo verius" judgements are absent, and the chapter closes with a list of the nine orders and "Et hec ... sufficiant", where the Cologne 1476, Rome 1481 and Blaubeuren 1474 prints agree with one another and pass to cap. 5. The abraded recto was not read. Manuscript catalogues were not searched for an abbreviated Manipulus with this ending.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 3/7
identification: Scholastic logic questions on genus, species and accident (Porphyrian predicables); work unidentified
note: Every line is torn on one side, so no complete clause survives ("specialissime", "generalissimam", "de accidentibus", "Ad aliam ad primam dicendum", "Solutio"). Google Books, Internet Archive and the Munich full text gave nothing and no candidate was reached for collation; this is genre only. The catalogue says paper; the support looks like parchment in the images.

identification: Not identified
note: Two strips, eight short lines in all, from a glossing exposition of Lenten matter: Christ's hunger ("esuriit .s. salutem") and "not by bread alone" (Matthew 4), and the Lord calling together his good soldiers. Twelve Corpus Corporum proximity searches across all four faces, Google Books and Internet Archive found only the general exegetical tradition (Hilary, Anselm of Laon), no text agreeing with a face. Probably an unprinted sermon or gloss.

identification: Exposition of Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), locus a divisione and the explicit of the tract; not a musical treatise; commentary unidentified
note: The recto ends an exposition of Tractatus V with the locus a divisione ("arguendo a posicione vnius membrorum diuidencium") and the scribe's "Et sic est finis quinti tractatus"; it follows F-21br in subject and is in the hand of F-7smu. The verso holds pen trials: the "staves" are three freehand lines with a few note-like marks, not readable notation. The wording matches none of the printed commentaries compared for F-21br. The lower two thirds of the recto rest mainly on the first reading.

identification: Exposition of Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), loci a maiori, a minori, a coniugatis, a casibus; not a musical treatise; commentary unidentified
note: Recto: topics a maiori and a minori with the stock example of king and knight taking a castle ("attribuendo duobus subiectis duo predicata"); verso: loci medii, a coniugatis and a casibus ("duo concreta, vnum nominale et alterum aduerbiale"). A research reader compared page images of Dorp 1499 and the Cologne Copulata 1494 and machine-read text of Versor, Georgius Bruxellensis, Tartaretus and Johannes de Magistris: the doctrine, order and examples agree, the sentences never do. The reading is at clause level; unprinted expositions were not searched. Same hand and work as F-7smu and F-hwsh.

identification: Not identified
note: Only one face is available: the catalogue links the same image to both canvases. The leaf is in the hand of the Tractatus V exposition on F-7smu, F-21br and F-hwsh but has other matter, a question with numbered conclusions on what is "scibile siue considerabile" in a science and on unity by aggregation. It is not a musical treatise. No complete sentence was secured and phrase searches found nothing. Questions on the Posterior Analytics or a Physics proem of the Buridan school are an untested lead.

identification: Charter: letter of institution to a benefice (issuer, place and date unread); not a literary text
note: A single-sheet fifteenth-century Latin letter of institution and investiture to a benefice at a place ending in "-kirchen", vacant by the death of one Andreas, on the presentation of a patron "dominus Henricus de [...]dorff", with a mandate to induct and a sealing clause. The issuer in line 1 is lost and the surname, place and date could not be read securely; a reading "Kranichberg / Prellenkirchen" was tested and rejected on the letter forms. Read by a research reader on the images; the verso shows only show-through. Better imaging of lines 3-9 and 24-25 would probably settle the names.

identification: Not identified
note: The spine strips carry numbered first-person questions on confession: whether all sins must be confessed, whether a priest may ever reveal a sin, whether one can confess through another, argued from profession and marriage. The order resembles the clauses of Omnis utriusque sexus. Phrase searches in Google Books, Internet Archive, Corpus Corporum, the Munich full text and the German manuscript catalogues found no text with this wording. What could be read on the 45 Da 6 head lining does not mention confession, so its belonging to the same text is not confirmed. Stopped for want of a candidate.

identification: Johannes Faventinus, Summa super Decretum Gratiani, pars I, D. 86 (comment on c. 8 Qui venatoribus to c. 24 Tanta nequitia)
note: Four passages on the spine strips (hunting in the arena, the Elisha narrative, the publicans with Misericordia plenitudo virtutum and Morte luitur, and the scheme of dispensation at Tanta nequitia) agree in wording and order with two manuscripts of the unprinted Summa, BAV Borgh. lat. 71 f. 57ra-57va and Reims BM 684 (openings f. 35v-36 and 36v-37), read on page images by a research reader; the coordinating model checked the publican passage against the Vatican page and the dispensation passage against the Reims page; no human review. The hunting passage is Stephen of Tournai's and the publican passage is Rufinus's in wording Stephen does not share, joined in one text and followed by a dispensation scheme that neither edition has at D. 86; the Elisha story is in both sources and separates nothing. Most of the fragment's differences from the Vatican copy recur in the Reims copy; two readings (exigunt ... sectantur with autem; movet for adducit) are matched in neither. The Summa Lipsiensis copies the dispensation scheme but differs in the hunting and publican passages; Simon of Bisignano, Sicardus, Tractaturus magister and Huguccio were not tested. Two panels are unread, and the script looks earlier than the catalogue's fourteenth century, recorded without redating.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
catalogue_title: Unidentified Roman law text, with gloss
identification: Justinian, Digestum vetus with the Accursian Glossa ordinaria, Digest 4.8.42-49 and 4.8.52-4.9.3 pr. (five of six strips placed, in one leaf)
note: Five of the six strips are placed in one two-column leaf (strip 3 is unplaced): line ends and beginnings on strips 2, 4, 5 and 6 agree in wording and sequence with Digest 4.8.45-49 on one page and 4.8.52, the rubric of 4.9 and 4.9.1-3 pr. on the other, with red initials at the inscriptions of Ulpian, Paulus and Julian. Five marginal glosses to D. 4.9.1 agree in wording and order with the Accursian ordinary gloss, and one is signed 'ac.' in the manuscript. A research reader compared the images with a transcription of Mommsen-Krueger for the text and with page images of the Paris 1566 glossed edition for the gloss; the coordinator read strip 2 'verso' and strip 6 'recto' against D. 4.9.1.1-2 and 1.7. Differences are slight: an apparent 'et' in the rubric, a probable omission supplied under one line, and two small variants in the gloss. Strip 3 and one face of strip 1 are unplaced, one column is abraded and barely read, the gloss was compared in one sixteenth-century print only, and Ms. 1033 was not examined.

identification: Prose gloss on Alexander de Villa Dei, Doctrinale, part III, vv. 2090-2096 (recto); commentary unidentified
note: The recto follows vv. 2090-2096 in order with two red lemmata (cedrinus, crastinus, acinum "lapillus in", perendino "a perendie", jacinctus, "Ante na"), compared by a research reader against machine-read text of Reichling's edition, not page images. The verso probably continues at vv. 2129-2134 but rests on doubtful lemmata. No named gloss (Admirantes, Glosa notabilis, printed commenta) was collated: untested, not excluded. The images are 1377 pixels wide, which limits the reading.

identification: Exposition or sermon on John 16:5-8 (fourth Sunday after Easter); work unidentified
note: Half-lines only: the Spirit as consolation, then a red "tertia pars" before "arguet mundum", explained as orderly reproof; the recto has a passage on a debtor and paradise and may belong to the previous Sunday. No connected phrase longer than three words survives, and Corpus Corporum, Google Books, Internet Archive, the Munich full text and Schneyer gave no candidate. Genre only.

identification: Guards from at least two manuscripts; one is a lemmatic commentary on Justinian, Institutes 4.6.35-38; commentary unidentified
note: Guards 17/18 and 5/6 join edge to edge into one column whose underlined lemmata follow Inst. 4.6.35-38 in order ("testamento in[tenderit]", "quam persequimur", "facultates / retentione / ipso iure / dotem", "cum parente"). Each lemma is short and several are uncertain, so the locus rests on the sequence; no whole gloss was read and the apparatus was compared only with poor machine-read text of the Accursian gloss in a 1607 print. A second hand on six guards and guard 113/114 were not read. The scans are about 640 pixels wide. The library's catalogue description was not consulted.

identification: Strips from a book of Latin sermons; one strip reworks the close of the Advent sermon Ps.-Augustine, Appendix 115; work unidentified
note: One strip paraphrases line by line, over seven lines, the closing exhortation of Ps.-Augustine, Sermo App. 115 section 5, a formula also carried by Ps.-Maximus, Sermo 1, and Rabanus, Homilia 1; compared by a research reader with the Corpus Corporum transcription only. The other three strips expound Luke 1:57-65 on the naming of John the Baptist in wording not found in print. A source of one passage is established; the book and the work are open.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: One face: passage on the fourfold sacrifice from the martyrs' sermon "Et quasi holocausti hostiam", printed as Anthony of Padua's; containing text not established
note: One face agrees, with small variants, with the moral reading of the fourfold sacrifice ("Ossa, qui fortitudinem et virtutem Deo attribuit et in eius servitio expendit") in the sermon on Wisdom 3:6 printed under Anthony of Padua's name in La Haye's edition (1739, p. 342), read on the page image by a research reader. The other face, citing Ezekiel 34 on the mountains of Israel, is not in that sermon or volume. The passage is absent from Anthony's Sermones dominicales et festivi, so the attribution is "printed as" only, and the strip may come from a source or from another sermon that reuses the passage. Two lines a face.

identification: Accursius, Glossa ordinaria on the Authenticum, Collatio IX: end of Ut iudices non expectent sacras iussiones (Nov. 125) and rubric to c. 1 of Ut litigantes iurent in exordio litis (Nov. 124); gloss only
note: The exposed strip is a gloss column: seven consecutive glosses (end of Sententiam, Iurent, De sportulis, Et ut que, Suffragium, Lites, Appellationes) match the 1566 Volumen legum parvum with Accursius, col. 471, in order and cross-references, and several are signed ac. in the fragment. A research reader compared the image with the page image of the print; no human review. Only line-ends of 6 to 12 letters are visible and one printed edition was compared; small differences of order and wording are recorded. The main text on the other face is not identified: a few words from a blurred photograph suggest the end of Nov. 120, a lead only.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea, Southern Middle Dutch translation of c. 1357 attributed to Petrus Naghel (Gulden legende), chapter on the dedication of a church (Vander wiinghen der kerken): end of the canonical hours to the seven sprinklings of the altar
note: Recto columns a and b, the last lines of verso column a and the upper strip of verso column b agree in wording and sequence with the Gulden legende as edited by W. Kuiper from Brussels KBR 15140 (ff. 398vb-399va), including 'Ten anderen sal men besien hoemense consacreert', the six acts of the altar consecration, the four kinds of charity with Genesis 28, and Christ's seven ways. A research reader compared the images with the edition's text of that one manuscript, not with manuscript images; the coordinator read recto column b lines 1-9 on the image. The leaf has Flemish spellings and a few single-word variants ('daermense met', 'bi huwelike', no 'eens', apparently no 'VII werven', 'lesen wi'). The catalogue's suggestion of Duranti's Rationale was tested on structure and by one Corpus Corporum search and is not supported; the Rationale was not collated at length. Most of the verso is too dark to read, and it is not established whether the leaf is already a recorded witness of the translation.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: (Pseudo-)Hugh of St Victor, Expositio in regulam sancti Augustini, Middle Dutch translation with the lemmata of the Rule, chapters 6-7 (PL 176, cols 899-904)
note: On all eight pages the Dutch follows the Latin of the Expositio sentence by sentence, lemma and commentary alike: the growth of sin and the psalm verse (col. 900), secret and public correction with 'pater des cloesters' for 'patri monasterii' (col. 903), and Gehazi and Naaman (col. 904). A research reader compared the images with PL 176, as page images for cols 901-904 and machine-read text for cols 899-900, rereading three of the eight pages; the coordinator read fol. [3]r on the image. The wording agrees closely with the Rooklooster translation edited by I. M. Kramp from Antwerp, Plantin-Moretus M 380, in five passages seen only as Google Books search snippets, with Flemish spelling and single-word differences ('ghenouchten' for 'gewoenten', 'pater' for 'uader', 'wreedelike rechten' for 'wreetliker daer ouer ordeelen'); the translation version is left open. The text sequence shows leaves [2] and [5] are consecutive and both precede [3] and [4], which does not fit the catalogue's numbering within one quire; this was not checked on the paper.

catalogue_title: Unidentified Middle Dutch Charlemagne romance, presumably Wybeert van Andernaken
identification: Not identified (the unique fragment edited by Stracke in 1927; no romance established)
note: These are the leaves D. A. Stracke edited as "Een onbekende Frankische roman" (Tijdschrift voor taal en letteren 15, 1927, 137-151); Kienhorst lists them as H129, unidentified. Three columns of the images agree with Stracke's text. The catalogue already cites the edition, and its "Wybeert van Andernaken" is a label for an otherwise unattested Middle Dutch poem on figures of the Narbonne cycle, not an identified romance. Phrase searches found no second witness; the fragments of Willem van Oringen and the Roman der Lorreinen were not collated, and DBNL full-text search was unavailable.

institution: Cambridge, MA, Harvard University, Houghton Library
catalogue_title: Unidentified poem on the passion addressed to Mary
identification: 'Die Freuden und Schmerzen Mariä' (anonymous German rhymed cycle), Seventh Sorrow; edited by Hamburger 2010 (identification already in the literature)
note: The Handschriftencensus (no. 22744, work 6704) lists Houghton MS Typ 270 as part of the only known copy of this anonymous cycle, and Hamburger 2010 prints the leaf's 42 lines; the text names itself as the seventh sorrow. A research reader reread the recto and the last 13 verso lines on the image against Hamburger's print, which shows only that this is the leaf he edits. The print has small slips (siebenden, deynen, forscht, war gewar, Dor er, mit in, Do der, Yemer). The grouping with four sister leaves, the Augsburg 1470s localisation and the derivation from Speculum humanae salvationis ch. 44-45 are Hamburger's and the census's and were not tested. Jörg Zobel's 'Von den Schmerzen Mariae' in Cgm 568 was read on images at three places and is a different poem; no second copy is known.
known_from: J. F. Hamburger, 'Typology Refigured', Harvard Library Bulletin 21.1-2 (2010), 73-94; Handschriftencensus no. 22744

institution: Cambridge, MA, Harvard University, Houghton Library
catalogue_title: Homiliary | Maximus of Turin, Homilia XC De poenitentia et jejuniis Ninivitarum I, sermon on penitence, and Gregory, Oratio ad plebem de mortalitate
identification: Caesarius of Arles, Sermo 144 (ed. Morin), In letaniis, De agenda paenitentia et Ninevitis, complete (inc. Evangelica lectio fratres carissimi dum legeretur); the sermon between the catalogue's Maximus and Gregory texts
note: The catalogue already identified the end of Maximus of Turin, Hom. XC, and the opening of Gregory's De mortalitate; the new part is the sermon between them, headed only 'Item unde supra', which is Caesarius, Sermo 144, complete from recto col. a line 15 to verso col. b line 21. A research reader compared the whole sermon with Morin's text in the OCR of the PL Supplementum 4 reprint (33 small variants, same order throughout) and read pp. 324-326 of Caillau's 1836 printing on page images; the coordinator read the opening on the image. The leaf's wording is that of the homiliary transmission (ut arbitror, purpuris deperire, short ending 'inculpabilis nemo est et immunis a reatu'), shared in part with Liverani's 1863 print from Roman and Florentine manuscripts, seen as snippets only. Morin held that Caesarius reworked an older unknown source; the leaf names no author. The homiliary type carrying this sequence is not established, Morin's own pages were not read as images, and recto col. b and verso col. a lines 1-33 rest on the first reading. No human review.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
catalogue_title: Unidentified chivalric romance, possibly Geraert van Viane
identification: Middle Dutch romance in couplets; not in the edited Geraert van Viane fragments or the Corpus Middelnederlands
note: The strip preserves four couplets from the heads of four columns of a Middle Dutch romance with a king and queen ("Sal ic bliuen ongehangen / Ende gine sult mi niet ontgangen"; "Des hadden si wonder groot / Ende die coninginne al bloot"). None of the lines is in the edited Geraert van Viane fragments or anywhere in the Corpus Middelnederlands. The content is compatible with the Aymeri-at-court episode of Girart de Vienne, for which no Dutch text survives, so the catalogue's suggestion stays possible and unproven. Not identified.

catalogue_title: St Cyprian, Sermon de la mortalité
identification: Cyprian, De mortalitate 8 and 11-12 in French; leaves B3 and B6 of one small-format edition in eights; translator and edition not identified
note: Both pieces come from one sheet of one book: envelope 7 is the top of leaf B6 and envelope 8 the foot of B3 and B6 of a small-format edition in eights, 22 lines to the page, carrying Cyprian, De mortalitate 8 and 11-12 in French. The translation is not the Frellon (1542), Tigeou (1574) or Goulart (1585) version; Belleforest's (1565) and the 1584 separate edition could not be seen. Edition and translator remain unidentified, so the result is partial. USTC was unreachable on the day.

identification: Sewing guards with a few letters a row; not legible in the published images
note: Not identified, because not legible in the published images. The catalogued fragment is a set of narrow parchment sewing guards at fol. 83 of a Latin sermon manuscript, with pale script of three to six letters per row; the best piece shows groups compatible with German ("nicht", "vnd") and nothing more. The first reader's text belongs to the two Latin host pages beside the guards, not to the fragment.

identification: Bible, Canticle of Moses (Audite caeli), Deuteronomy 32:1-27, Vulgate; book type (psalter with canticles, breviary or Bible) not established
note: The strip keeps 4-6 letters of each of 28 lines a face; about 40 of the 56 line fragments fall in Deut 32:1-27 in unbroken order at a steady interval of about 50 characters, and the four coloured initials stand at the openings of verses 8, 12, 23 and 26. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with a Vulgate transcription, and with page images of the Clementine text in Dereser 1788 for verses 7-11, 16-18 and 22-25; the coordinator read a selection of lines on both faces. No difference of wording is visible, and the strip cannot show the form of the Vulgate text (at v.17 'is e', as read, agrees with daemoniis and not daemonibus; one reading of three letters). About fifteen lines are uncertain, the catalogue's verso is the textual recto, and the kind of book is not established. No human review.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 6/7
identification: Scholastic notes, probably on a Trinitarian or Christological point; not identified
note: Paper scrap with the right half of about twenty lines of abbreviated scholastic notes, probably on a Trinitarian or Christological point ("a duobus ex distinctis", "procedit filius simpliciter"), followed by a divider and a new note; the verso is blank. No source found in Corpus Corporum, Google Books or Internet Archive searches; the reading is too fragmentary to test a candidate. Left unidentified.

identification: Pieces II-III (12th century): Daniel 9:16-17, Vulgate; kind of book not established. Pieces I and IV (14th century) unidentified
note: The two 12th-century pieces (II and III) carry Vulgate Daniel 9:16-17 in consecutive lines of one column; the match is exact apart from spelling, but nothing shows whether the book was a Bible or a lectionary. The two 14th-century pieces (I and IV) are a narrow vertical slice and a margin edge of a heavily abbreviated text, possibly legal or penitential, and remain unidentified. Status for the record as a whole: partial (one of two source manuscripts identified as to text).

identification: Moral-exegetical prose with a spiritual exposition of Joshua 11:10-11; work unidentified
note: Fragm. 95 b is a strip of moral-exegetical prose: one face urges contempt of something "harmful" with Job 20:27-28 and the rich men of Luke 12 and 16, the other expounds Joshua 11:10-11 spiritually (Joshua takes Asor and strikes souls with love). No printed text matched in Google Books, the Munich library, the Internet Archive or Hugh of St Cher's Postilla. The sibling Fragm. 95 a (F-gwts) is catalogued as Aquinas on the Sentences IV d. 44-45 and is a different, later text. Not identified; an unprinted Joshua commentary such as Langton's is the lead to test.

identification: All Saints sermon on Congregate illi sanctos eius (Ps 49:5); opening agrees with the incipit of Nicolaus de Byard, Sermones de sanctis no. 194 (Schneyer IV p. 244; also under Robert of Sorbon, Schneyer V no. 2016); body not collated
note: Two strips from a two-column fourteenth-century sermon collection. The flourished initial opens an All Saints sermon on Congregate illi sanctos eius whose first sentence matches Nicolaus de Byard, Sermones de sanctis no. 194 (Schneyer IV p. 244; also in Robert of Sorbon's collection, BnF lat. 15951 f. 336rb). Only that opening, five part-lines, was compared, against the repertory incipit and a printed quotation; the body and the collection are unverified, so partial.

identification: Aegidius de Fuscarariis, Ordo iudiciarius, cc. LXIX (Conclusio causae, second half) - LXX (Forma sententiae diffinitivae, opening); ed. Wahrmund pp. 124-126
note: Both pieces come from one two-column leaf and agree with Wahrmund's edition in wording and order over about 33 partial lines on each of two consecutive columns, including the author's opinion on the assessors' fee, the citations in sequence, the red chapter rubric and the model sentence of the archpriest of Bologna. A research reader reread every line on enlarged images and compared them with page images of pp. 124-126, text and apparatus; the coordinator checked passages on both faces of strip A against p. 125. Differences are few (rubric as in the edition's MS B, 'cuius malitie' as in M and V, 'et habebis', and as read 'dicte mulieris' as in P); they are recorded without a claim about the fragment's place in the tradition. Piece B supplies the other half of the first nine lines of strip A's columns, and the catalogue's recto/verso labels for B are opposite to those for A. Some rubbed lines were read only in part; no human review.

identification: Canonistic text on marriage, after 1215 (impediments, spiritual kinship, nuptial blessing); work unidentified
note: Fragm. 128 is a strip of a two-column leaf from a canonistic text on marriage of after 1215: one column on impediments ending with spiritual kinship ("actiones non passiones ... acquiritur uiro", citing C. 30 q. 4 and X 4.7), another on the nuptial blessing and priests at mass, citing De clandestina desponsatione, perhaps from a treatment of second marriages. Citations are underlined; no lemmata were seen. William of Rennes and Raymund, Tancred, Hostiensis's Summa, Goffredus, Innocent IV, Johannes Andreae, the Abbas antiquus and the ordinary gloss on C. 30 and on X 4.21 c. 1 were compared in OCR or by search and do not match. The faint, tiny script gave no secure run of words to search even after a second reading, so the work is unidentified.

identification: Office lectionary, Assumption octave to the Decollation of John the Baptist: Song of Songs, Paschasius Radbertus Cogitis me, Passio Bartholomaei (BHL 1002), Bede on Luke 22, Petrus Chrysologus Sermo 127; one lesson and five scraps unplaced
note: Fifteen binding scraps from an unnoted office lectionary of about 1200, long lines, covering the Assumption octave to the Decollation of John the Baptist. Its lessons are Song of Songs 2-3 and 5, Paschasius Radbertus's Cogitis me, the Passio Bartholomaei (BHL 1002, abridged), Bede on Luke 22:28-29 and Petrus Chrysologus Sermo 127; the Fragmentarium description already had the Canticle, Paschasius and Chrysologus and assigned the Bede passage to Amalarius. Nine of the scraps join into three leaves of three cuttings per line. One Assumption lesson and five scraps remain unidentified; status partial because of those unplaced parts.

identification: Psalms 149:1-4 and 149:8-150:3 in Geert Grote's Middle Dutch translation (as in his Getijdenboek, ed. Van Wijk 1940, pp. 46-47), on each of two leaves; probably a book of hours, kind of book and unity of the leaves not established
note: On three of four faces the surviving middle of ten to twelve consecutive lines agrees in wording and order with Psalms 149-150 in Van Wijk's edition of Grote's hours ('die dochteren van [Syon hoghe vr]ouwen', '[eendrachtigh]en versamenden sa[nghe]', 'en die sachtmo[dighen]', '[hei]lighen louet de[n] / te sinre crachte[n] / crachten louet'); the psalter of the 1360 Bible translation words the same verses differently and is excluded. A research reader reread those lines on enlargements of the low-resolution native images with the source beside them and compared them with the DBNL transcription of the edition and Google Books snippets, not page images; the coordinator read fol. [2]r lines 6-12 and fol. [2]v lines 6-11 and agrees. Differences are dialectal (hem, wel, -voudicheit for the edition's oen/sich, wal, -uoldicheit). Whether the two leaves come from one codex is open, and Grote's psalms also circulated in complete psalters (Van den Berg 1942, p. 262), so a book of hours is probable, not shown; BNM-I was unreachable (login), and the Fragmentarium and MMFC records list no literature. No human review.

identification: Fifteenth-century scholastic text; too little legible to search
note: A narrow strip of a fifteenth-century cursive scholastic text, cut to ten to fifteen letters a line and imaged too coarsely to read connected words. Only isolated words (Dico, religione, officium, ubique) are legible. Unidentified; needs a better image before any search is worth running.

identification: Third-declension noun paradigms (mater, soror, homo, omnis) in the form of the elementary grammar Ianua; version not established
note: The strips hold third-declension noun paradigms in the form used by the Italian elementary grammar Ianua (Ps.-Donatus): mater, soror, homo, omnis and probably felix. Donatus's Ars minor is excluded. The series does not match the three printed Ianua editions compared (Rome c. 1475, Venice c. 1478 and 1491), which lack soror, so the result is partial: the type of text and its place are known, the exact recension is not.

dimensions: 171 mm x 50 mm, 55 mm x 35 mm, 58 mm x 30 mm
institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Thirteenth-century text under tissue and a later breviary; no connected word legible
note: The 13th-century text stays unidentified: it is visible only under tissue, in a torn window about 3 cm wide and along one cut edge, and no connected word could be read. The legible writing in the images is the 15th-century breviary F-x3dh (Lenten chapters and collect, Palm Sunday antiphons). The split between the two records was fixed from their stated dimensions: the 171 x 50 mm piece is the covered spine strip in the larger hand. New imaging or separation of the layers is needed before any search.

institution: Leuven, Archief van de Abdij van Park
identification: Latin article on almsgiving (Elemosina) from a preaching aid, in paragraphs opening 'Elemosina debet ...'; work unidentified
note: Latin; an article on almsgiving in a preaching aid, in paragraphs each beginning "Elemosina debet ...", two of which survive in part ("fieri prouidenter", "dari [pauperibus]"). The paragraph on the poor runs parallel in matter and order to Bromyard, Summa praedicantium, Elemosina art. 7, but not in wording, and Byard, Peraldus and the Alphabetum narrationum were tested and rejected. The work is unidentified; the upper third of both faces is illegible in the published image.

catalogue_date: at earliest 1300 CE; at earliest 1349 CE
identification: German spiritual prose on compassion (2 Cor 11:29, 1 Cor 12:26); work unidentified
note: Not identified. Strip across a single-column bifolium of a small German prose book, first half of the 14th century, same binding campaign as F-28bq: a first-person passage on sharing a neighbour's trouble and weakness (2 Cor 11:29) and St Paul's saying that when one member suffers all suffer (1 Cor 12:26). The Handschriftencensus (no. 27263) lists it as an unidentified "Geistlicher Prosatext". No match in ReM, Google Books, Internet Archive or the sermon and mystical editions searched.

catalogue_date: at earliest 1300 CE; at earliest 1349 CE
identification: German spiritual prose: the Son's report to the Father and the Father's love for the Son; work unidentified
note: Not identified. Strip across a single-column bifolium of a small German prose book (first half of the 14th century, Central German spellings): the Son reports to the Father that he has fulfilled his commandment and redeemed mankind with his blood, and the Father is said to owe the Son the highest love because he is God. The Handschriftencensus (no. 27263) lists it with F-m05m as an unidentified "Geistlicher Prosatext". ReM, Google Books, Internet Archive and a dozen sermon and mystical editions gave no match.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 14/7
identification: Commentary on the topics from conjugates and cases, probably on Peter of Spain, Tractatus V; commentary unidentified
note: The strip is from a commentary on the topics "from conjugates and cases", most probably on Peter of Spain's Tractatus V: the verso rejects "album est dulce, ergo albedo est dulcedo" and the recto reports what the "antiqui" say. Dorp's commentary on Buridan and Versor's on Peter of Spain were read on the page and are not the text, though they share its examples. Partial: the kind of work and its place are known, the commentary is not.

identification: Strip on a binding with about ten rows of writing visible only as blurred bands; not legible in the published images
note: The strip on the spine of MdS 63 Ea 7 shows rows of writing only as blurred bands on all three published images, in every colour channel and after contrast processing. No letter was read and no search was possible. The catalogue's description as a glossed legal text could not be tested. New imaging is required before another attempt.

identification: Gregorian sacramentary, Advent orations: Suscipiamus, Excita ... saluari, the six 'Aliae orationes de adventu' (Excita ... operare, Conscientias, Prope esto, Concede ... ut magnae, Mentes nostras, Preces populi tui), Porrige nobis, Deus qui nos conspicis; kind of book open
note: A strip 4-6 letters wide: all 36 letter groups (20 lines on the recto, 16 on the verso) fall in order, one per line, in this series of Advent prayers, with 16-36 supplied letters between groups, and the text continues across the turn of the leaf. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with page images of Wilson's Hadrianum (pp. 113, 116-117) and Mohlberg's St Gall 348 (p. 216); the coordinator reread recto lines 5-14 and verso lines 6-15. The strip has the Hadrianum order 'promisisti usque in finem saeculi'; the last two prayers are from the Gelasian Advent series, and the opening pair is not in the Hadrianum's mass order. It is not the same manuscript as Fragm. 3a of the same host volume (9 mm lines against 5-6 mm, different hand). Whether the book was a sacramentary, missal or collectar is open; the evidence is positional, on letter groups only.

identification: Scholastic passage on the guilt of Christ's crucifiers (ending with 1 Cor 2:8) and a pastoral passage; work unidentified
note: Fol. [2]r has a passage on the guilt of Christ's crucifiers ending with 1 Cor 2:8 ("filium dei", "ac rebelles", "offenderunt", "populares", "maiores" legible), the matter of Aquinas ST III q. 47 a. 5-6 but not his wording; fol. [1]r is on another, pastoral subject ("nemo ambigit", "Abbas", "celebrare", "de clericis"). No connected phrase is secure enough to search and seven phrase searches found nothing. Stop: needs UV or infrared images of the line beginnings.

identification: Paper leaf in thin grey cursive; letter groups only, no searchable phrase
note: Both faces inspected at reading size; the thin grey ink gives only letter groups, with repeated line openings ("q'") suggesting a list, verses or notes. The hand looks like that of HS.2583/084 (F-vui8), which carries Ave verum corpus, but no text could be confirmed here and no search was possible. Stop: needs UV or infrared images.

identification: Elevation prayer Ave verum corpus natum in the last four lines of the written face; the lines above and the collection unidentified
note: The last four lines of the written face (canvas 0, native box 1350,2100-4200,2850) are the elevation prayer Ave verum corpus (AH 54 no. 167), read on the image over three continuous lines and compared with the standard text from printed prayer books (OCR and snippets). The lines above it and the left page are unread, so the collection the leaf comes from is not identified; the catalogue's "theological text" is better described as devotional notes. A better image of lines 1-12 would show whether an indulgence rubric precedes the prayer.

identification: Question commentary of the arts faculty: 'Consequenter queritur utrum multiplicatio individuorum sub eadem specie repugnet animabus separatis', preceded by a question on the first being; work unidentified
note: Four paper pieces from a late fourteenth-century scholastic question series. One question opening was read on the image: Consequenter queritur utrum multiplicatio individuorum sub eadem specie repugnet animabus(?) separatis, with an argument that the first being either willed and could not, or could and did not will, several individuals in one species. It follows a question on the first being under a metaphysical and a physical habit. There is no second heading and no lemma. A search index of Zimmermann's lists of Metaphysics commentaries and Siger's questions on the Liber de causis do not have the question in this wording, so the work stays unidentified.

identification: Scholastic questions on confession within an exposition of a base text; same book as MdS 45 Da 5 (F-3u3b, F-ho7z); work unidentified
note: The three linings of MdS 45 Da 6 belong with those of 45 Da 5 (F-3u3b, F-ho7z): first-person questions on confession inside an exposition of a base text, with a passage on an "edification" that falls if its foundation is moved. Phrase searches in Google Books, Internet Archive, Corpus Corporum and MDZ found nothing; the Astesana was read and rejected, the other confessors' summae rejected on form without collation. Reading is model-assisted; the large strip F2 is photographed too obliquely to read below line 7.

identification: Third-declension paradigms (mater, soror, homo, omnis, fortis, fortior) in the order of the elementary grammar Ianua, with a soror paradigm found in no Ianua text compared; one leaf with MdS 58 Ca 19/F1-2 (F-uvx5; reconstruction F-5oah)
note: Foot of a leaf with third-declension paradigms in the Ianua form: mater and soror on the recto, the end of fortis and fortior on the verso. It is one of three slices of the same leaf: MdS 58 Ca 19/F2 (plural of soror, then homo) is the head of the verso and F1 (omnis, start of fortis) its middle, so F-fuvo, F-uvx5 and F-5oah are one object, not independent witnesses. The series mater, homo, omnis, fortis, fortior is that of the pseudo-Donatan Ianua (Ciccolella 2008, snippets; mater also on the page image of the Rome c. 1475 print); soror is in no Ianua text reached. Not Donatus's Ars minor; a manuscript form of the Ianua with soror is likely but unproved.

identification: Spine strips showing mid-line word fragments only; no searchable phrase
note: Only short mid-line fragments are exposed on two of the three strips, and the legible one (F1) is upside down in the images, which the first reading missed. An upright rereading gives a few words ("ymagini", "sua", a red-touched S) but no searchable phrase; one guess at Apocalypse 13 found no support.

identification: Justinian, Codex 7.62.31-32 (De appellationibus), with marginal gloss; second strip probably C. 7.65.8
note: Strip [1] recto has five consecutive line ends of C. 7.62.31 pr. and the verso four of five line beginnings of C. 7.62.32.1-1a, one column later, read by a research reader on the images and compared with page images of Krueger 1877, the Leipzig 1831 edition and a glossed Paris 1559 edition; the coordinator read the key words on both faces. Only spelling differences were seen; verso line 3 could not be confirmed. Strip [2] recto probably has C. 7.65.8 (two pieces, with an unexplained blank between them) and its verso is not placed. The gloss is too rubbed to identify; the Accursian gloss at this point is compatible with the one clear word, spectabil-.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Accursius, Glossa ordinaria on the Digestum vetus, gloss "illatae sunt" to D. 4.9.1.8 (strip 1)
note: Strip 1 "recto" carries five cut lines of the Accursian ordinary gloss on illatae sunt (D. 4.9.1.8): "est contrarium / -nque. §. quod si servus. et de hiis / vel al. ... l. i. et / ... / l. sequitur", agreeing in wording and order with the Paris 1566 print, col. 663 gloss h, which a research reader read on the page image; the coordinator read lines 1, 2, 3 and 5 on the manuscript crops. No "C." was seen before "de hiis", line 4 is unread under the liturgical offset, and line 5 is faint beyond "l. s.q.". This is the paragraph and gloss column of the sibling leaf Ms. 1032 (F-x60p), and the gloss column of that leaf's strip 5 keeps other words of the same gloss ("fug. qui-", "-is qui la-", weakly read) that appear complementary, so the strip very probably belongs to that leaf; the hands are compatible but no physical join was fitted. Strip 2 shows no legal text, the liturgical offset was not studied, and source-assisted image comparison also confirms the diagnostic citation sequence in Venice 1488, BSB scan 202, and Vatican Pal. lat. 731, fol. 86v (catalogued Bologna, 1290-1300). Both earlier witnesses have the second C. before de hiis; the fragment's apparent omission remains unresolved. No new letters were recovered and no textual-family relationship is claimed.

identification: Abridgement of William of Auxerre, Summa aurea III (faith, hope, charity); shares three compressions word for word with the abbreviation in Troyes, Médiathèque, Ms. 1966, which catalogues give to Herbert of Auxerre, but has passages that copy lacks
note: The strip is from an abbreviation of William of Auxerre's Summa aurea, book III (faith, hope, charity; Paris 1500 print fols. 136r-139r). It shares three compressed passages word for word with Troyes, Ms. 1966, ff. 108r-109r, catalogued as Herbert of Auxerre's Abbreviatio, and these are not William's wording as read on page images of the print. Two passages give abridged replies of William that the Troyes copy lacks, and no second Herbert manuscript could be read (Erfurt CA 8° 29 is behind an access challenge), so the result stays at medium confidence. The catalogue's verso precedes its recto.

identification: Six lines of cursive a face, illegible at the published size beyond 'ad sepulcra martirum'; work unidentified
note: The published images (about 2,400 px for the whole photograph) allow only isolated words: the recto is illegible, and the verso yields "ad sepulcra martirum" (probable) and possibly the names Cyprianus and Jeronimus opening rubricated items. Phrase searches in Corpus Corporum, Internet Archive, Google Books and MDZ found only the patristic sources of that phrase, and no candidate work was collated. A higher-resolution or UV capture is needed before another attempt.

identification: Two bifolia washed to a faint ghost; no connected line legible in the published images
note: Both bifolia are washed to a faint ghost on all four faces; contrast enhancement, background division and channel separation on the native images recover only the tall strokes of a small two-column cursive, and no connected line. Nothing was searched. UV or multispectral images are needed before another attempt.

catalogue_title: Unidentified Middle Dutch manuscript, possibly a religious text
identification: Middle Dutch saints' lives (Petronilla, probably Nicholas) divided by rubrics Prima, Secunda, Tercia [lectio?]; neither the Northern nor the Southern Dutch Legenda aurea; work unidentified
note: Six strips from a Middle Dutch book of saints' legends in numbered sections (red rubrics Prima / Secunda / [Ter]cia ...ctio, probably lectio; a red number lxxxx). One strip has the Petronilla legend and another probably the Nicholas story of the poor nobleman's daughters. Both passages were compared on page images with the Southern (Delft 1482 Passionael) and Northern (Gent UB HS.0123) translations of the Legenda aurea and match neither, so the text is another version, likely office lessons; the containing work was not found.

identification: Small-format book arranged by Sundays after Pentecost ('Dominica xiiij, Mattheus', Mt 6:24; Dominica xi, Mc 7); sermons or postil, work unidentified
note: The four spine strips come from a small 14th-century book arranged by the Sundays after Pentecost: red rubrics "Do(minica) xj. M[ar.]" (F4) and "Do(minica) xiiij. Math." (F3) can be read, the latter followed by "[Nemo potest] duobus dominis servire" (Mt 6:24), which matches Roman/Franciscan pericope numbering and the catalogue's Mc 7:32 on F4. The suggested reading "dist. xiiij ... magister" (Sentences commentary) does not hold. The body text is out of focus in every photograph, so the work (sermons, postil or thematic outlines) is not identified; better photographs of F3 and F4 are needed.

identification: Besides the catalogued Isidore, Etymologiae I: five lines before De soloecismo that end De barbarismo with matter on conlisio and hiatus not in Isidore's text; source unidentified
note: The unidentified text is five lines at the top of fol. 1r, the end of a chapter on barbarism that replaces or expands Isidore's Etym. 1.32.8-9: an L-alliteration example, conlisiones with Virgil (read as Aen. 5.866) and a second example, and the sentence "Hiatus vero et conlisiones per vocales et consonantes fiunt". It is not the standard Isidore text, not Julian of Toledo, and not in Zofingen Pa 32 or St. Gallen 237, which were read on the page; Spevak's 2017 study of additions to book I reports nothing at this point, and Pompeius offers parallels of content only. The leaf may come from a school copy of book I (Ars Isidori) with added Donatus-commentary material; that is a lead, not a finding.

identification: Trimmed leaf in a small faint hand; no secure word sequence at the published resolution
note: The strip occupies only about 650 x 1650 pixels of each published image, with lines 12-15 px high; contrast enhancement in three treatments on both faces gave letter groups but no readable word sequence, so no search was possible. The limit is image resolution as much as abrasion; a higher-resolution capture from the Erfgoedbibliotheek would reopen it.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 17/7
identification: Rules of consequence on the integral whole; one rule ('a toto integrali distributo ad partem distributam') is closely parallel to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3 c. 3, the only text found with it; dependence not shown; work unidentified
note: The recto has the rule "Alia regula est a toto [integrali] distributo ad partem distributam est consequentia bona", a close parallel in shortened wording to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3, c. 3; the neighbouring lines do not follow Ockham's text. Albert of Saxony, Buridan with Dorp, the pseudo-Ockham Elementarium and Tractatus minor, Burley and Greve were compared and do not have the distributed rule; Marsilius and Strode were not reached. One shared rule with differing context and untested alternatives is a promising connection, not shown dependence; the work is not identified.

identification: Avicenna, Canon medicinae (Latin of Gerard of Cremona), III, fen 3, tract. 1, end of ch. 1 (De anatomia oculi) and rubric of ch. 2
note: Strip A keeps only the first or last few letters of the bottom 24 lines of two columns; 22 of 24 line ends on one side and all 24 line beginnings on the other, ending in the rubric [com]plexionum eius, stand in the order and spacing of Canon III.3.1.1-2 in the Padua 1479 print. A research reader compared them with the print's page images; the coordinator read the first eleven line beginnings of canvas 0 on the native image and lines 1-19 of that side on the print's pages. One doubtful reading (similiter for the print's simile) could not be decided; only one print was compared and the attribution of the translation to Gerard of Cremona is the conventional one, not checked. Strip B carries only a marginal scheme. The catalogue's 'probably a treatise on optics' is corrected to medical anatomy of the eye.
